title: Microsoft, DepEd launch AI literacy program for 2,000 teachers

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Microsoft and the Department of Education (DepEd) have partnered to train 2,000 public school teachers in artificial intelligence (AI) literacy through a professional development program launched on November 5 in Makati City.
The Microsoft Elevate for Educators program aims to equip teachers with the skills to integrate AI into classroom instruction while promoting responsible technology use and human oversight.
Around 100 senior high school teachers attended the event and participated in a day of hands-on training at the Microsoft Philippines office.

“Through our work with the Department of Education, we are seeing how AI is changing what is possible in education—from how teachers design learning experiences to how students explore ideas and prepare for future opportunities,” said Caroline Foo, Managing Director of Microsoft Philippines.
“But the future will demand more than knowing how to use new tools. It will require judgment, adaptability and a strong sense of responsibility,” Foo added.

Teachers to undergo AI training through 2027
Through its partnership with DepEd and training partner Audentes Technologies, the program aims to train and credential 2,000 Filipino public school teachers in AI literacy over the coming months.

Participating educators will undergo instructor-led training and earn digital badges, while gaining access to a free Microsoft Elevate for Educators credential developed with ISTE+ASCD and aligned with the AI Literacy Framework.
The program also gives teachers access to a global community of more than 100,000 educators, allowing them to exchange knowledge, share classroom practices and learn from fellow educators.
Training activities will continue through two virtual sessions in November 2026, followed by eight live learning sessions from January to May 2027.

Alongside the training program, Microsoft introduced Behind the Chat and the AI Classroom Toolkit, which provide classroom-ready materials to help educators discuss digital privacy, critical thinking, and responsible online behavior with students. (By David Buenaventura, INQUIRER.net Intern)
